finding.claim: SQL injection in /search. The unauthenticated query parameter `q` is interpolated into the SQL string with an f-string. An attacker can break out of the LIKE literal and run UNION SELECT queries against any table in shop.db (for example sqlite_master or user and credential tables). They can also use boolean or error-based extraction. Python's sqlite3 execute() rejects multiple statements, so stacked queries are not possible, but UNION-based data exfiltration is.
finding.source: request.args.get('q') on the public GET /search route, with no authentication
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") on a sqlite3 connection

trace.note: Flask route /search, public ingress with no auth decorator
term = request.args.get('q', '') takes attacker-controlled input with no validation
term is interpolated directly into the SQL text via an f-string and executed
Results are returned as JSON, so UNION-selected data is reflected to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: No input validation or escaping on `term`. No parameterization on this query (the other two queries at lines 18 and 25 do use `?` placeholders). No authentication, authorization, WAF or middleware anywhere in the app. No length limit. The route is public ingress under Flask defaults. The only mitigation is sqlite3 refusing multi-statement execution, which does not stop UNION-based extraction. Repro: GET /search?q=' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master--

verdict.reason: app.py:11-12 passes the anonymous `q` parameter straight into an f-string SQL query on the public /search route (app.py:9) with no auth, validation or parameterization, and app.py:13 returns the rows as JSON, so UNION extraction works; the two-column SELECT also matches the proposed UNION payload.
